raw_evidence.label: 311 launched in 2003 — the first call was a noise complaint
raw_evidence.content: New York City's 311 hotline was inaugurated by Mayor Michael Bloomberg on March 9, 2003 as the non-emergency counterpart to 911, consolidating roughly 40 city call centers and hotlines into a single number. The very first call to NYC311, at 12:01 AM on launch day, was a noise complaint from Jackson Heights, Queens. Through 2023 the system had received more than 525 million inquiries from New Yorkers, 68% by phone, 28% on the web, 3% in the mobile app (launched 2013), and the remainder through text and other channels. Every row in this dataset is one of those calls, web tickets, or app submissions — each one a New Yorker formally telling the city that something is too loud.

raw_evidence.label: Dataset scale
raw_evidence.content: Two full calendar years of noise-related 311 service requests yields 1,439,558 rows — every formally filed noise complaint in New York City between 2023-01-01 and 2024-12-31. The data is unusually tidy for a city open-data dump: eight values of complaint_type, 31 descriptors, 230 distinct ZIP codes, and only four responding agencies (NYPD, DEP, EDC, and a single ghost row coded to 3-1-1 itself).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_01: Dataset scale ---
print("=== ana_01 ===")
n_rows = len(df)
n_complaint_types = df["complaint_type"].nunique()
n_descriptors = df["descriptor"].nunique()
n_zips = df["incident_zip"].nunique()
n_agencies = df["agency"].nunique()
print(f"rows: {n_rows:,}")
print(f"complaint_type values: {n_complaint_types}")
print(f"descriptor values: {n_descriptors}")
print(f"distinct ZIP codes: {n_zips}")
print(f"distinct responding agencies: {n_agencies}")
print(f"date range: {df['created_date'].min()}  to  {df['created_date'].max()}")
raw_evidence.output:
rows: 1,439,558
complaint_type values: 8
descriptor values: 31
distinct ZIP codes: 230
distinct responding agencies: 4
date range: 2023-01-01 00:00:42  to  2024-12-31 23:59:33

raw_evidence.label: Year-over-year: noise complaints rose 9.8% from 2023 to 2024
raw_evidence.content: Noise complaints rose from 686,283 in 2023 to 753,275 in 2024 — a 9.8% year-over-year increase and an extra 67,000 complaints. The 2024 average is 2,058 complaints per day (2024 was a leap year), versus 1,880 per day in 2023. (Note: this figure is below the 19% year-over-year jump some 2024 press coverage reported, because press counts often draw a slightly different filter from the same dataset.)
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_02: Year-over-year volume (2023 vs 2024) ---
print("=== ana_02 ===")
df["year"] = df["created_date"].dt.year
yc = df["year"].value_counts().sort_index()
print("Noise complaints per calendar year:")
for y, c in yc.items():
    print(f"  {int(y)}: {c:,}")
delta = yc[2024] - yc[2023]
pct = 100 * delta / yc[2023]
print(f"  Δ (2024 − 2023): {delta:+,}  ({pct:+.1f}%)")
print(f"  daily average 2023: {yc[2023] / 365:.0f}")
print(f"  daily average 2024: {yc[2024] / 366:.0f}  (2024 was a leap year)")
raw_evidence.output:
Noise complaints per calendar year:
  2023: 686,283
  2024: 753,275
  Δ (2024 − 2023): +66,992  (+9.8%)
  daily average 2023: 1880
  daily average 2024: 2058  (2024 was a leap year)

sentences.summary: det_04: Which agency handles which complaint — the routing logic behind every row. Source: Noise Complaints — NYC311 portal (https://portal.311.nyc.gov/article/?kanumber=KA-02125) Facts: Different complaint sub-types are routed to different agencies; NYPD handles residential, neighbor, and vehicle noise complaints Source: 311 Noise Complaint NYC: How to File, Which Agency Handles It (HelpNewYork 2026) (https://helpnewyork.com/how-to-file-noise-complaint-nyc/) Facts: NYPD officers must witness the noise in progress to issue a violation; Many residential noise complaints close as 'observed no evidence of violation' if noise has stopped before arrival

raw_evidence.label: Which agency handles which complaint — the routing logic behind every row
raw_evidence.content: Every noise complaint is automatically routed by 311 to one of three city agencies based on its complaint_type. The NYPD owns the residential, street/sidewalk, and vehicle/horn buckets — the bulk of the dataset — and dispatches a patrol unit that must physically witness the violation to issue a summons; if the noise has stopped by the time officers arrive, the request typically closes with 'observed no evidence of the violation.' The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) handles construction, commercial, music venue, and ice cream truck complaints, sending field inspectors with sound meters during permit hours — often days later. The Department of Transportation (DOT) takes a small slice (mostly highway/bridge noise). The agency column in the data is therefore as much a story about what enforcement is even possible as about who is complaining.

raw_evidence.label: Complaint-type ranking — Residential is half of everything
raw_evidence.content: Noise – Residential is by far the largest bucket at 47.1% of all complaints (677,749). Street/Sidewalk noise is second at 21.6% (310,450), Commercial third at 9.5% (136,096), the generic 'Noise' top-level (which mostly contains construction-noise descriptors) is fourth at 7.5%, Vehicle is fifth at 6.9%, Helicopter sixth at 6.1%, then a small Park slice (1.2%) and an even smaller House of Worship slice (0.18%). The two top categories together — Residential plus Street — are 69% of every formal noise grievance in New York.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_04: Complaint-type distribution ---
print("=== ana_04 ===")
ct = df["complaint_type"].value_counts()
total = len(df)
print(f"All complaint_type values, 2023 + 2024 combined ({total:,} rows):")
for label, count in ct.items():
    pct = 100 * count / total
    print(f"  {count:>9,}  {pct:>5.2f}%  {label}")
raw_evidence.output:

raw_evidence.label: Which agency handles which complaint — the routing logic behind every row
raw_evidence.content: Every noise complaint is automatically routed by 311 to one of three city agencies based on its complaint_type. The NYPD owns the residential, street/sidewalk, and vehicle/horn buckets — the bulk of the dataset — and dispatches a patrol unit that must physically witness the violation to issue a summons; if the noise has stopped by the time officers arrive, the request typically closes with 'observed no evidence of the violation.' raw_evidence.label: Agency split — NYPD owns 86% of noise, EDC quietly owns helicopter

DEP takes 108,234 (7.5%) — the entire generic 'Noise' bucket, which is essentially all construction-noise descriptors. EDC (the city's Economic Development Corporation, which owns the heliports) takes 87,813 (6.1%) — every single Helicopter complaint. One stray complaint in the data is coded to '3-1-1' itself.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_06: Responding agency split ---
print("=== ana_06 ===")
ag = df["agency"].value_counts()
print("Complaints by responding agency (2023 + 2024 combined):")
for label, count in ag.items():
    pct = 100 * count / total
    print(f"  {count:>9,}  {pct:>5.2f}%  {label}")

# Agency × complaint_type cross-tab — which agency owns which buckets
print("\nAgency × complaint_type (counts):")
crosstab = pd.crosstab(df["complaint_type"], df["agency"])
crosstab = crosstab.loc[ct.index]  # order by overall volume
crosstab["TOTAL"] = crosstab.sum(axis=1)
print(crosstab.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: The NYPD response pattern — 'observed no evidence of the violation'
raw_evidence.content: For residential, vehicle, and street noise the NYPD must physically observe an active violation to write a summons — and by the time officers arrive, the party is usually over. The first row in the raw CSV (case 56416252, January 1 2023, 12:00 AM, Sedgwick Avenue, Bronx) closed seventeen and a half hours later with the resolution text 'The Police Department responded to the complaint and with the information available observed no evidence of the violation at that time.' Across all NYC agencies, 'Did Not Observe'–style closures account for roughly 25% of 311 closures; the NYPD's share on residential noise specifically is higher. This dataset's resolution_description column is therefore where you read what the city actually did about each call — not just whether something was filed.

raw_evidence.label: Response time — NYPD closes in 41 minutes, DEP in 3 days, EDC takes 35 days
raw_evidence.content: Median time from created_date to closed_date varies by three orders of magnitude depending on the agency. NYPD closes the median noise complaint in 0.68 hours (41 minutes), and 90% of NYPD cases close within 3.91 hours. DEP, which handles construction and ice cream truck calls, takes a median 68.3 hours (2.85 days) with a p90 of 251.78 hours (10.5 days). EDC, which owns every helicopter complaint, takes a median 843.23 hours — over 35 days — to close a request, with a p90 of 2,746 hours (114 days). Across complaint types within each agency the response time is essentially flat, because what determines speed is who answers, not what the problem is.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_16: Response time by agency × top complaint type ---
print("=== ana_16 ===")
# trim crazy negative or absurdly long values (1y) before computing summary stats
clean = closed[(closed["response_hours"] >= 0) & (closed["response_hours"] <= 24 * 365)]
print(f"closed complaints with valid response_hours: {len(clean):,} / {len(df):,}")

# Median + 90th-percentile response time by agency
print("\nResponse-time summary by responding agency (closed cases only):")
agg = (
    clean.groupby("agency", observed=True)["response_hours"]
    .agg(["count", "median", lambda s: s.quantile(0.9)])
    .rename(columns={"<lambda_0>": "p90_h"})
)
agg = agg.sort_values("count", ascending=False)
for ag_label, row in agg.iterrows():
    print(f"  {ag_label:<6}  n={int(row['count']):>9,}  median={row['median']:>8.2f} h  p90={row['p90_h']:>9.2f} h")

print("\nMedian response (h) by complaint_type × agency:")
ct_top = clean["complaint_type"].value_counts().head(8).index
ag_top = clean["agency"].value_counts().head(4).index
sub = clean[clean["complaint_type"].isin(ct_top) & clean["agency"].isin(ag_top)]
pivot = sub.pivot_table(values="response_hours", index="complaint_type", columns="agency", aggfunc="median", observed=True)
pivot = pivot.loc[ct_top]
print(pivot.round(2).to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Which agency handles which complaint — the routing logic behind every row
raw_evidence.content: Every noise complaint is automatically routed by 311 to one of three city agencies based on its complaint_type. The NYPD owns the residential, street/sidewalk, and vehicle/horn buckets — the bulk of the dataset — and dispatches a patrol unit that must physically witness the violation to issue a summons; if the noise has stopped by the time officers arrive, the request typically closes with 'observed no evidence of the violation.' The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) handles construction, commercial, music venue, and ice cream truck complaints, sending field inspectors with sound meters during permit hours — often days later. The Department of Transportation (DOT) takes a small slice (mostly highway/bridge noise). The agency column in the data is therefore as much a story about what enforcement is even possible as about who is complaining.

raw_evidence.label: The NYPD response pattern — 'observed no evidence of the violation'
raw_evidence.content: For residential, vehicle, and street noise the NYPD must physically observe an active violation to write a summons — and by the time officers arrive, the party is usually over. The first row in the raw CSV (case 56416252, January 1 2023, 12:00 AM, Sedgwick Avenue, Bronx) closed seventeen and a half hours later with the resolution text 'The Police Department responded to the complaint and with the information available observed no evidence of the violation at that time.' Across all NYC agencies, 'Did Not Observe'–style closures account for roughly 25% of 311 closures; the NYPD's share on residential noise specifically is higher. This dataset's resolution_description column is therefore where you read what the city actually did about each call — not just whether something was filed.

raw_evidence.label: Response time — NYPD closes in 41 minutes, DEP in 3 days, EDC takes 35 days
raw_evidence.content: Median time from created_date to closed_date varies by three orders of magnitude depending on the agency. EDC, which owns every helicopter complaint, takes a median 843.23 hours — over 35 days — to close a request, with a p90 of 2,746 hours (114 days). Across complaint types within each agency the response time is essentially flat, because what determines speed is who answers, not what the problem is.

sentences.summary: det_05: Channel mix — the slow death of the 311 phone call. Source: NYC311 — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NYC311) Facts: Through 2023: 68% phone, 28% web, 3% mobile app, 1% other; Mobile app launched in 2013 Source: 311 Services — NYC Council Data Team (https://council.nyc.gov/data/311-services/) Facts: Phone remained the dominant channel through 2023; Web (NYC311 website) is the second-largest channel and has grown steadily over the past five years

raw_evidence.label: Channel mix — the slow death of the 311 phone call
raw_evidence.content: Although the dataset still spans phone, online, mobile app, and 'other' submissions, the channel mix shifts every year. Across the whole city, of 525 million 311 inquiries through 2023, 68% came in by phone, 28% by web, 3% through the NYC311 mobile app, and 1% by text or other channels. The mobile app launched in 2013 but only crossed a few percent of total share a decade later. The 'open_data_channel_type' column in this dataset is therefore one of the cleanest measures of a slow-motion habit change: which New Yorkers still dial 311 when their upstairs neighbor throws a party at 2 AM, and which open the app or load 311.nyc.gov.

raw_evidence.label: Channel shift 2023 → 2024 — online down 15 pp, mobile and phone up
raw_evidence.content: The biggest year-over-year shift is in how complaints get filed, not what they say. ONLINE share dropped 15 percentage points between 2023 and 2024 (68.8% → 53.5%), while MOBILE rose 8 pp (22.6% → 30.5%) and PHONE rose 7 pp (8.6% → 15.9%). In absolute terms ONLINE complaints actually fell by 69,000 even though the dataset grew overall, while MOBILE added 75,000 and PHONE more than doubled (59K → 120K). The mobile app and the dialled-in voice call are both gaining at the website's expense — a non-obvious result given the widespread story that 311 is going more digital.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: Channel shift, 2023 vs 2024 ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
df["year"] = df["created_date"].dt.year
ch_y = pd.crosstab(df["open_data_channel_type"], df["year"])
ch_y_pct = ch_y / ch_y.sum() * 100
print("Channel share by year (%):")
for ch_label, row in ch_y_pct.iterrows():
    p23 = row[2023]
    p24 = row[2024]
    delta = p24 - p23
    print(f"  {ch_label:<10}  2023: {p23:5.2f}%   2024: {p24:5.2f}%   Δ {delta:+.2f} pp")
print("\nChannel absolute counts by year:")
for ch_label, row in ch_y.iterrows():
    print(f"  {ch_label:<10}  2023: {row[2023]:>8,}   2024: {row[2024]:>8,}")

raw_evidence.label: Per-capita hot spots — where complaint density is highest
raw_evidence.content: Several outside analyses have mapped 311 noise complaints per capita rather than per zip. A 2018 RentHop study using NYC Open Data found Hamilton Heights to be the noisiest neighborhood in the city at 0.0486 complaints per resident, with Marble Hill/Inwood (0.0481) second — both more than 10x the Upper East Side. The NYS Comptroller's longer-window analysis (2010–2015) found Washington Heights/Inwood the highest at ~82 noise complaints per 1,000 adults per year. TimeOut reported the Bronx as the loudest borough in 2025 per capita, with Wakefield and Fordham specifically. Different windows highlight different leaders, but Upper Manhattan and the Bronx consistently top the per-capita list — a pattern any per-zip or per-borough chart from this dataset should reproduce.

raw_evidence.label: Who complains — gentrification, racial boundaries, and the demographics of dialling 311
raw_evidence.content: A widely cited 2016 study, 'Contested Boundaries: Explaining Where Ethnoracial Diversity Provokes Neighborhood Conflict' by Joscha Legewie (NYU) and Merlin Schaeffer, used 4.7 million geo-coded 311 service requests and showed that neighbor-conflict 311 complaints (noise, public drinking, blocking driveways) spike along 'fuzzy' racial/ethnic boundaries — transitional blocks between two more homogeneous communities — rather than at sharp boundaries. Subsequent journalism by Marketplace, Gothamist, BuzzFeed, and Pacific Standard documented that per-capita 311 calls in gentrifying NYC neighborhoods grew 70% faster than the city average; noise calls grew 'twice as fast in gentrifying neighborhoods as in high-income enclaves and 50 percent faster than in poor districts.' The CRITICAL caveat for any analysis: 311 measures who complains, not where noise is actually loudest, and 311 does not record the demographics of the caller.

raw_evidence.label: Borough share — Manhattan tops raw count, but the Bronx is loudest per capita
raw_evidence.content: By raw complaint volume the boroughs are close: Manhattan 26.9% (387,561), Brooklyn 26.2% (377,416), Bronx 24.7% (354,909), Queens 20.0% (287,977), Staten Island 2.2% (31,157). Per 1,000 residents the order flips dramatically: the Bronx files 241 complaints per 1,000 residents over two years, Manhattan 229, Brooklyn 138, Queens 120, and Staten Island only 63 — Staten Islanders complain less than one-quarter as much per person as Bronx residents. That ordering matches the recent TimeOut finding that the Bronx was the loudest borough by per-capita complaint rate in 2025.

    pct = 100 * count / total
    print(f"  {count:>9,}  {pct:>5.2f}%  {label}")

# 2020 American Community Survey 5-year population estimates by NYC borough
# (these are baseline for per-capita scaling; integers in residents)

    "BRONX": 1_472_654,

}

    c = int(bo.get(b, 0))
    per1k = 1000 * c / pop
    print(f"  {b:<14}  {c:>8,} complaints  / {pop:>9,} residents = {per1k:>6.1f} per 1k")

raw_evidence.label: Per-capita hot spots — where complaint density is highest
raw_evidence.content: Several outside analyses have mapped 311 noise complaints per capita rather than per zip. A 2018 RentHop study using NYC Open Data found Hamilton Heights to be the noisiest neighborhood in the city at 0.0486 complaints per resident, with Marble Hill/Inwood (0.0481) second — both more than 10x the Upper East Side. The NYS Comptroller's longer-window analysis (2010–2015) found Washington Heights/Inwood the highest at ~82 noise complaints per 1,000 adults per year. TimeOut reported the Bronx as the loudest borough in 2025 per capita, with Wakefield and Fordham specifically. Different windows highlight different leaders, but Upper Manhattan and the Bronx consistently top the per-capita list — a pattern any per-zip or per-borough chart from this dataset should reproduce.

raw_evidence.label: Who complains — gentrification, racial boundaries, and the demographics of dialling 311
raw_evidence.content: A widely cited 2016 study, 'Contested Boundaries: Explaining Where Ethnoracial Diversity Provokes Neighborhood Conflict' by Joscha Legewie (NYU) and Merlin Schaeffer, used 4.7 million geo-coded 311 service requests and showed that neighbor-conflict 311 complaints (noise, public drinking, blocking driveways) spike along 'fuzzy' racial/ethnic boundaries — transitional blocks between two more homogeneous communities — rather than at sharp boundaries. Subsequent journalism by Marketplace, Gothamist, BuzzFeed, and Pacific Standard documented that per-capita 311 calls in gentrifying NYC neighborhoods grew 70% faster than the city average; noise calls grew 'twice as fast in gentrifying neighborhoods as in high-income enclaves and 50 percent faster than in poor districts.' The CRITICAL caveat for any analysis: 311 measures who complains, not where noise is actually loudest, and 311 does not record the demographics of the caller.

Subsequent journalism by Marketplace, Gothamist, BuzzFeed, and Pacific Standard documented that per-capita 311 calls in gentrifying NYC neighborhoods grew 70% faster than the city average; noise calls grew 'twice as fast in gentrifying neighborhoods as in high-income enclaves and 50 percent faster than in poor districts.' The CRITICAL caveat for any analysis: 311 measures who complains, not where noise is actually loudest, and 311 does not record the demographics of the caller.

raw_evidence.label: ZIP 10466 — one complaint every 17 seconds on its worst day, 99% via mobile app
raw_evidence.content: The 10466 anomaly isn't a slow drip — it's a series of huge bursts almost entirely funneled through the NYC311 mobile app. On Sunday 2024-09-15, the ZIP filed 4,952 complaints in 24 hours — one every 17.4 seconds, all day, every hour. 4,933 of those (99.6%) came through MOBILE; only 13 through the website and 6 by phone. Eight separate days in 2024 saw 3,000+ complaints from this single ZIP, all with the same channel distribution. The median day in 10466 is 12 complaints; on its top day it is 412× that. Across the eighteen days with 1,000+ complaints, the pattern is identical: an avalanche of mobile-app filings flagged 'Loud Music/Party,' suggesting an organized mass-filing or a very small group of repeat reporters rather than a real noise spike.

# --- ana_25: 10466 noisiest single days + channel ---

top10 = daily_z.nlargest(10)
print(f"10466 single-day top 10:")
for d, c in top10.items():
    sub = z[z["day"] == d]
    by_ch = sub["open_data_channel_type"].value_counts()
    mobile = int(by_ch.get("MOBILE", 0))
    online = int(by_ch.get("ONLINE", 0))
    phone = int(by_ch.get("PHONE", 0))
    print(f"  {d.date()}  total={c:>5,}   mobile={mobile:>5,}  online={online:>4,}  phone={phone:>4,}")

# Rate metric: on the Sep 15 spike day, complaints per second
peak_day = top10.idxmax()
peak_count = int(top10.iloc[0])
seconds = 86400
rate = peak_count / seconds
print(f"\nOn {peak_day.date()}, 10466 logged {peak_count:,} complaints in 24h — one every {seconds/peak_count:.1f} seconds.")

# Median complaints per day in 10466 vs every other day
median_z = daily_z.median()
print(f"\n10466 median complaints per day:    {median_z:.0f}")
print(f"10466 mean   complaints per day:    {daily_z.mean():.0f}")
print(f"10466 days above 1000 complaints:   {(daily_z > 1000).sum()}")

print(f"10466 days above 3000 complaints:   {(daily_z > 3000).sum()}")

raw_evidence.label: Channel mix — the slow death of the 311 phone call
raw_evidence.content: Although the dataset still spans phone, online, mobile app, and 'other' submissions, the channel mix shifts every year. Across the whole city, of 525 million 311 inquiries through 2023, 68% came in by phone, 28% by web, 3% through the NYC311 mobile app, and 1% by text or other channels. raw_evidence.label: Channel mix — the slow death of the 311 phone call
raw_evidence.content: Although the dataset still spans phone, online, mobile app, and 'other' submissions, the channel mix shifts every year. Across the whole city, of 525 million 311 inquiries through 2023, 68% came in by phone, 28% by web, 3% through the NYC311 mobile app, and 1% by text or other channels. The mobile app launched in 2013 but only crossed a few percent of total share a decade later. The 'open_data_channel_type' column in this dataset is therefore one of the cleanest measures of a slow-motion habit change: which New Yorkers still dial 311 when their upstairs neighbor throws a party at 2 AM, and which open the app or load 311.nyc.gov.

raw_evidence.label: Per-capita hot spots — where complaint density is highest
raw_evidence.content: Several outside analyses have mapped 311 noise complaints per capita rather than per zip. A 2018 RentHop study using NYC Open Data found Hamilton Heights to be the noisiest neighborhood in the city at 0.0486 complaints per resident, with Marble Hill/Inwood (0.0481) second — both more than 10x the Upper East Side. The NYS Comptroller's longer-window analysis (2010–2015) found Washington Heights/Inwood the highest at ~82 noise complaints per 1,000 adults per year. TimeOut reported the Bronx as the loudest borough in 2025 per capita, with Wakefield and Fordham specifically. Different windows highlight different leaders, but Upper Manhattan and the Bronx consistently top the per-capita list — a pattern any per-zip or per-borough chart from this dataset should reproduce.

raw_evidence.label: ZIP 10466 — one complaint every 17 seconds on its worst day, 99% via mobile app
raw_evidence.content: The 10466 anomaly isn't a slow drip — it's a series of huge bursts almost entirely funneled through the NYC311 mobile app. On Sunday 2024-09-15, the ZIP filed 4,952 complaints in 24 hours — one every 17.4 seconds, all day, every hour. 4,933 of those (99.6%) came through MOBILE; only 13 through the website and 6 by phone. Eight separate days in 2024 saw 3,000+ complaints from this single ZIP, all with the same channel distribution. The median day in 10466 is 12 complaints; on its top day it is 412× that. Across the eighteen days with 1,000+ complaints, the pattern is identical: an avalanche of mobile-app filings flagged 'Loud Music/Party,' suggesting an organized mass-filing or a very small group of repeat reporters rather than a real noise spike.

    by_ch = sub["open_data_channel_type"].value_counts()
    mobile = int(by_ch.get("MOBILE", 0))

# Rate metric: on the Sep 15 spike day, complaints per second

# Median complaints per day in 10466 vs every other day

print(f"10466 days above 2000 complaints:   {(daily_z > 2000).sum()}")

raw_evidence.label: Channel mix — the slow death of the 311 phone call
raw_evidence.content: Although the dataset still spans phone, online, mobile app, and 'other' submissions, the channel mix shifts every year. Across the whole city, of 525 million 311 inquiries through 2023, 68% came in by phone, 28% by web, 3% through the NYC311 mobile app, and 1% by text or other channels. The mobile app launched in 2013 but only crossed a few percent of total share a decade later. The 'open_data_channel_type' column in this dataset is therefore one of the cleanest measures of a slow-motion habit change: which New Yorkers still dial 311 when their upstairs neighbor throws a party at 2 AM, and which open the app or load 311.nyc.gov.

raw_evidence.label: Per-capita hot spots — where complaint density is highest
raw_evidence.content: Several outside analyses have mapped 311 noise complaints per capita rather than per zip. A 2018 RentHop study using NYC Open Data found Hamilton Heights to be the noisiest neighborhood in the city at 0.0486 complaints per resident, with Marble Hill/Inwood (0.0481) second — both more than 10x the Upper East Side. The NYS Comptroller's longer-window analysis (2010–2015) found Washington Heights/Inwood the highest at ~82 noise complaints per 1,000 adults per year. TimeOut reported the Bronx as the loudest borough in 2025 per capita, with Wakefield and Fordham specifically. Different windows highlight different leaders, but Upper Manhattan and the Bronx consistently top the per-capita list — a pattern any per-zip or per-borough chart from this dataset should reproduce.

raw_evidence.content: The 10466 anomaly isn't a slow drip — it's a series of huge bursts almost entirely funneled through the NYC311 mobile app. On Sunday 2024-09-15, the ZIP filed 4,952 complaints in 24 hours — one every 17.4 seconds, all day, every hour. 4,933 of those (99.6%) came through MOBILE; only 13 through the website and 6 by phone. Eight separate days in 2024 saw 3,000+ complaints from this single ZIP, all with the same channel distribution. The median day in 10466 is 12 complaints; on its top day it is 412× that. Across the eighteen days with 1,000+ complaints, the pattern is identical: an avalanche of mobile-app filings flagged 'Loud Music/Party,' suggesting an organized mass-filing or a very small group of repeat reporters rather than a real noise spike.

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter noise exploded between 2020 and 2023
raw_evidence.content: Helicopter noise is the only sub-category whose absolute volume has multiplied by orders of magnitude in the past four years. The NYC Council's helicopter-noise data team found that 311 complaints rose from 811 in January 2020 to 7,461 in May 2023 alone, and tallied 59,127 complaints for all of 2023. The driver was the return of tourism: in May 2023, 8,848 helicopter flights moved over NYC land or water, of which 1,929 were sightseeing tours from the Downtown Manhattan Heliport and 1,398 were tour flights from Linden, NJ. The flights that produced the most complaints per flight were non-tour rides to/from JFK and West 30th Street (0.77 complaints per flight) and tour flights from Linden (0.57 per flight). The complaint hotspots are not at the heliports themselves but along the flight paths: the Upper West Side, Central Park, Murray Hill–Kips Bay in Manhattan, and Carroll Gardens–Cobble Hill–Gowanus–Red Hook plus Prospect Heights/Park Slope in Brooklyn.

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter complaints fell 51% from 2023 to 2024 — opposite of the prior trend
raw_evidence.content: Despite the City Council's own data team reporting 59,127 helicopter-noise complaints for 2023, the 2024 number is just 28,686 — a 51.5% drop, the largest year-over-year decline of any complaint_type. Every single month except September is down year-over-year, often by half or more (May fell from 7,461 to 2,833; December fell from 8,724 to 2,843). This contradicts the prior 2020 → 2023 explosion documented by Stop the Chop and the Council, and is the strongest argument in the dataset that something changed around early 2024 — either filings tactics, public attention, or weather/flight volume — well before the 2025 Helicopter Oversight Act passed.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_19: Helicopter complaints by month, 2023 vs 2024 ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
heli = df[df["complaint_type"] == "Noise - Helicopter"]
print(f"Total helicopter-noise complaints, 2023+2024: {len(heli):,}")
heli_y = heli["year"].value_counts().sort_index()
print(f"  2023: {int(heli_y.get(2023, 0)):,}")
print(f"  2024: {int(heli_y.get(2024, 0)):,}")
print(f"  Δ: {int(heli_y.get(2024, 0) - heli_y.get(2023, 0)):+,}   ({100*(heli_y.get(2024,0)-heli_y.get(2023,0))/heli_y.get(2023,1):+.1f}%)")
heli_month = heli.groupby(["year", "month"]).size().unstack("year").fillna(0).astype(int)
print("\nMonthly helicopter complaints, 2023 vs 2024:")
print(heli_month.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter noise exploded between 2020 and 2023
raw_evidence.content: Helicopter noise is the only sub-category whose absolute volume has multiplied by orders of magnitude in the past four years. The NYC Council's helicopter-noise data team found that 311 complaints rose from 811 in January 2020 to 7,461 in May 2023 alone, and tallied 59,127 complaints for all of 2023. The driver was the return of tourism: in May 2023, 8,848 helicopter flights moved over NYC land or water, of which 1,929 were sightseeing tours from the Downtown Manhattan Heliport and 1,398 were tour flights from Linden, NJ. The flights that produced the most complaints per flight were non-tour rides to/from JFK and West 30th Street (0.77 complaints per flight) and tour flights from Linden (0.57 per flight). The complaint hotspots are not at the heliports themselves but along the flight paths: the Upper West Side, Central Park, Murray Hill–Kips Bay in Manhattan, and Carroll Gardens–Cobble Hill–Gowanus–Red Hook plus Prospect Heights/Park Slope in Brooklyn.

raw_evidence.label: Stop the Chop and the 2025 Helicopter Oversight Act
raw_evidence.content: The advocacy group Stop the Chop NY NJ has been pushing for years to ban non-essential helicopter operations at the two city-owned heliports — East 34th Street and Downtown Manhattan (renamed Downtown Skyport in April 2025). On April 24, 2025 the City Council passed the Helicopter Oversight Act (Intro 26-A), sponsored by Majority Leader Amanda Farías: starting in 2029 the two city-owned heliports may only host helicopters that meet the FAA's strictest noise standards, exempting law enforcement, emergency response, news, and film production. The bill passed two weeks after six people died when a sightseeing helicopter crashed into the Hudson River. The 2023–2024 noise data is therefore the baseline that motivated the change.

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter complaints fell 51% from 2023 to 2024 — opposite of the prior trend
raw_evidence.content: Despite the City Council's own data team reporting 59,127 helicopter-noise complaints for 2023, the 2024 number is just 28,686 — a 51.5% drop, the largest year-over-year decline of any complaint_type. Every single month except September is down year-over-year, often by half or more (May fell from 7,461 to 2,833; December fell from 8,724 to 2,843). This contradicts the prior 2020 → 2023 explosion documented by Stop the Chop and the Council, and is the strongest argument in the dataset that something changed around early 2024 — either filings tactics, public attention, or weather/flight volume — well before the 2025 Helicopter Oversight Act passed.

print(f"Total helicopter-noise complaints, 2023+2024: {len(heli):,}")
heli_y = heli["year"].value_counts().sort_index()
print(f"  2023: {int(heli_y.get(2023, 0)):,}")
print(f"  2024: {int(heli_y.get(2024, 0)):,}")
print(f"  Δ: {int(heli_y.get(2024, 0) - heli_y.get(2023, 0)):+,}   ({100*(heli_y.get(2024,0)-heli_y.get(2023,0))/heli_y.get(2023,1):+.1f}%)")
heli_month = heli.groupby(["year", "month"]).size().unstack("year").fillna(0).astype(int)
print("\nMonthly helicopter complaints, 2023 vs 2024:")
print(heli_month.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter hotspots — 58% Manhattan, ZIP 10023 alone is 31%
raw_evidence.content: Helicopter complaints are spatially concentrated in a way the other categories are not. Manhattan files 57.8% of every helicopter complaint (50,743 of 87,813), Queens 23.9%, Brooklyn 16.8%, and the Bronx and Staten Island under 1% combined. The single ZIP 10023 — Upper West Side / Lincoln Center / Riverside Park — accounts for 27,539 complaints, 31% of all helicopter complaints citywide. The next biggest, 11414 in Howard Beach Queens (close to the JFK approach), files 16,646. This concentration aligns with the Council data team's hotspot list of Upper West Side, Murray Hill–Kips Bay, and the Carroll Gardens / Park Slope strip along the Hudson and East Rivers.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_20: Helicopter borough hotspots ---
print("=== ana_20 ===")
heli_bo = heli["borough"].value_counts(dropna=False)
total_heli = len(heli)
for label, count in heli_bo.items():
    print(f"  {count:>7,}  {100*count/total_heli:>5.2f}%  {label}")

# top zips for helicopter
print("\nTop 15 ZIPs for helicopter complaints:")
zip_h = heli.dropna(subset=["incident_zip"]).copy()
zip_h["incident_zip"] = zip_h["incident_zip"].str.zfill(5)
zh_counts = zip_h["incident_zip"].value_counts().head(15)
for z, c in zh_counts.items():
    b = zip_h.loc[zip_h["incident_zip"] == z, "borough"].mode()
    b_str = str(b.iloc[0]) if len(b) else "?"
    print(f"  {z}  {c:>5,}  {b_str}")

raw_evidence.content: Helicopter noise is the only sub-category whose absolute volume has multiplied by orders of magnitude in the past four years. The NYC Council's helicopter-noise data team found that 311 complaints rose from 811 in January 2020 to 7,461 in May 2023 alone, and tallied 59,127 complaints for all of 2023. The driver was the return of tourism: in May 2023, 8,848 helicopter flights moved over NYC land or water, of which 1,929 were sightseeing tours from the Downtown Manhattan Heliport and 1,398 were tour flights from Linden, NJ. The flights that produced the most complaints per flight were non-tour rides to/from JFK and West 30th Street (0.77 complaints per flight) and tour flights from Linden (0.57 per flight). The complaint hotspots are not at the heliports themselves but along the flight paths: the Upper West Side, Central Park, Murray Hill–Kips Bay in Manhattan, and Carroll Gardens–Cobble Hill–Gowanus–Red Hook plus Prospect Heights/Park Slope in Brooklyn.

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter complaints fell 51% from 2023 to 2024 — opposite of the prior trend
raw_evidence.content: Despite the City Council's own data team reporting 59,127 helicopter-noise complaints for 2023, the 2024 number is just 28,686 — a 51.5% drop, the largest year-over-year decline of any complaint_type. Every single month except September is down year-over-year, often by half or more (May fell from 7,461 to 2,833; December fell from 8,724 to 2,843). This contradicts the prior 2020 → 2023 explosion documented by Stop the Chop and the Council, and is the strongest argument in the dataset that something changed around early 2024 — either filings tactics, public attention, or weather/flight volume — well before the 2025 Helicopter Oversight Act passed.

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter noise exploded between 2020 and 2023
raw_evidence.content: Helicopter noise is the only sub-category whose absolute volume has multiplied by orders of magnitude in the past four years. The NYC Council's helicopter-noise data team found that 311 complaints rose from 811 in January 2020 to 7,461 in May 2023 alone, and tallied 59,127 complaints for all of 2023. The driver was the return of tourism: in May 2023, 8,848 helicopter flights moved over NYC land or water, of which 1,929 were sightseeing tours from the Downtown Manhattan Heliport and 1,398 were tour flights from Linden, NJ. The flights that produced the most complaints per flight were non-tour rides to/from JFK and West 30th Street (0.77 complaints per flight) and tour flights from Linden (0.57 per flight). The complaint hotspots are not at the heliports themselves but along the flight paths: the Upper West Side, Central Park, Murray Hill–Kips Bay in Manhattan, and Carroll Gardens–Cobble Hill–Gowanus–Red Hook plus Prospect Heights/Park Slope in Brooklyn.

raw_evidence.label: Helicopter complaints fell 51% from 2023 to 2024 — opposite of the prior trend
raw_evidence.content: Despite the City Council's own data team reporting 59,127 helicopter-noise complaints for 2023, the 2024 number is just 28,686 — a 51.5% drop, the largest year-over-year decline of any complaint_type. raw_evidence.label: Fireworks summers — the seasonal noise signal that explains big late-June spikes
raw_evidence.content: Two seasonal events dominate every annual noise chart: the late-June into July-4 illegal fireworks wave, and the Memorial-Day weekend warmup. Fireworks complaints rose 2,429% during July 4–6 2020 vs. the same days in 2019 — 10,801 in three days — and summer 2020 logged 47,000+ fireworks complaints, sixty times 2019. The wave never fully receded: ~18,000 in summer 2021, ~7,000 each in summers 2022 and 2023. These appear in the dataset under complaint_type 'Noise' (the generic top-level category) with descriptor 'Banging/Pounding' or 'Fireworks'; expect a visible spike every late June, peaking on July 4, in any 2023 or 2024 chart.

print("\nHour-of-day, weekend nights (Fri+Sat) vs weekday nights (Mon-Thu+Sun):")
weekend = df.loc[df["dow"].isin(["Friday", "Saturday"]), "hour"].value_counts().sort_index()

weekend_per_day = weekend / (df.loc[df["dow"].isin(["Friday", "Saturday"]), "created_date"].dt.normalize().nunique())
weekday_per_day = weekday / (df.loc[df["dow"].isin(["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Sunday"]), "created_date"].dt.normalize().nunique())
print(f"  hour   wkday/d   wknd/d   wknd÷wkday")
for h in range(24):
    wd = weekday_per_day.get(h, 0)

    ratio = we / wd if wd else 0
    print(f"  {h:>2}:00  {wd:>7.0f}   {we:>7.0f}   {ratio:>5.2f}")

raw_evidence.label: The July 4 fireworks pulse — visible in 2023, much flatter in 2024
raw_evidence.content: In 2023 the late-June / early-July fireworks wave is clearly visible: June 24–25 produced 3,550 then 4,150 complaints (vs the dataset median of 1,684), and July 4 itself hit 3,607. In 2024 the spike spread out and softened — June 22–23 reached 2,974 then 3,359, and July 4 was 3,252 — slightly above an average day rather than the dramatic stand-out it was in 2023. The dataset contains no descriptor literally tagged 'firework' in 2023–2024 (fireworks roll into Banging/Pounding and other descriptors), so this pulse has to be read off the daily counts and the calendar rather than off a category.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_15: Late-June fireworks pulse — daily complaints around July 4 ---
print("=== ana_15 ===")
# Look at June 20 → July 8 each year
window_2023 = df[(df["created_date"] >= "2023-06-20") & (df["created_date"] < "2023-07-09")]
window_2024 = df[(df["created_date"] >= "2024-06-20") & (df["created_date"] < "2024-07-09")]
print("Daily complaint count, late-June into July 8, each year:")
print(f"  {'date':<12}  {'2023':>8}  {'date':<12}  {'2024':>8}")
d23 = window_2023.groupby(window_2023["created_date"].dt.normalize()).size()
d24 = window_2024.groupby(window_2024["created_date"].dt.normalize()).size()
days = list(d23.index) if len(d23) else []
for d in days:
    matching_2024 = pd.Timestamp(year=2024, month=d.month, day=d.day)
    c23 = d23.get(d, 0)
    c24 = d24.get(matching_2024, 0)
    print(f"  {d.date()}  {c23:>8,}  {matching_2024.date()}  {c24:>8,}")

# fireworks descriptor share
print("\nFireworks-related descriptors, all years, all months:")
firework_mask = df["descriptor"].astype(str).str.contains("Firework", case=False, na=False)
print(f"  fireworks-tagged complaints: {firework_mask.sum():,}")
fw = df.loc[firework_mask]
fw_month = fw.groupby([fw["created_date"].dt.year, fw["created_date"].dt.month]).size()
print("\nFireworks complaints by year-month (only months with ≥10):")
for (y, m), c in fw_month.items():
    if c >= 10:
        print(f"  {int(y)}-{int(m):02d}: {c:>5,}")

raw_evidence.label: Fireworks summers — the seasonal noise signal that explains big late-June spikes
raw_evidence.content: Two seasonal events dominate every annual noise chart: the late-June into July-4 illegal fireworks wave, and the Memorial-Day weekend warmup. Fireworks complaints rose 2,429% during July 4–6 2020 vs. the same days in 2019 — 10,801 in three days — and summer 2020 logged 47,000+ fireworks complaints, sixty times 2019. The wave never fully receded: ~18,000 in summer 2021, ~7,000 each in summers 2022 and 2023. These appear in the dataset under complaint_type 'Noise' (the generic top-level category) with descriptor 'Banging/Pounding' or 'Fireworks'; expect a visible spike every late June, peaking on July 4, in any 2023 or 2024 chart.

raw_evidence.label: The NYPD response pattern — 'observed no evidence of the violation'
raw_evidence.content: For residential, vehicle, and street noise the NYPD must physically observe an active violation to write a summons — and by the time officers arrive, the party is usually over. The first row in the raw CSV (case 56416252, January 1 2023, 12:00 AM, Sedgwick Avenue, Bronx) closed seventeen and a half hours later with the resolution text 'The Police Department responded to the complaint and with the information available observed no evidence of the violation at that time.' Across all NYC agencies, 'Did Not Observe'–style closures account for roughly 25% of 311 closures; the NYPD's share on residential noise specifically is higher. This dataset's resolution_description column is therefore where you read what the city actually did about each call — not just whether something was filed.

raw_evidence.label: Why this data became politically central — the NYPD Quality of Life Division
raw_evidence.content: On April 9, 2025 — shortly after the period this dataset covers — Mayor Eric Adams and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch launched a new NYPD Quality of Life Division ('Q-Teams') focused on noise, derelict vehicles, illegal mopeds, and other 311 complaint types. Officers received training on sound metering devices specifically for noise enforcement. The pilot improved non-emergency response times by 47 minutes on average citywide. By August 2025 Q-Teams were rolled out in every precinct in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island. The 2023–2024 noise data is the pre-Q-Team baseline; future cuts of the same dataset will show whether response times shortened and 'no evidence observed' closures fell after the division stood up.

raw_evidence.label: Ice cream truck jingles — a category where enforcement essentially does not happen
raw_evidence.content: One unusually specific corner of the data is the 'Ice Cream Truck' descriptor under DEP. Under a 1970s-era deal with the City Council, ice cream trucks are allowed to play their jingle while moving but not while stopped, with fines from $350 to $3,000. Gothamist reported 7,000+ Mister Softee jingle complaints over four years (through 2014) and 1,013 in the first half of 2016 alone — but only one ticket was issued. The mismatch is structural: DEP inspectors arrive days after the call, by which point the truck is gone. This dataset will let us see how big that complaint stream still is in 2023–2024 and whether DEP's resolution status has changed.

Only 1,891 of 677,749 residential noise complaints (0.28%) end with a summons or violation issued. In practical terms: when you file a residential noise complaint in NYC, the chance that an officer documents a citable violation is fewer than 3 in 1,000.

raw_evidence.label: The NYPD response pattern — 'observed no evidence of the violation'
raw_evidence.content: For residential, vehicle, and street noise the NYPD must physically observe an active violation to write a summons — and by the time officers arrive, the party is usually over. The first row in the raw CSV (case 56416252, January 1 2023, 12:00 AM, Sedgwick Avenue, Bronx) closed seventeen and a half hours later with the resolution text 'The Police Department responded to the complaint and with the information available observed no evidence of the violation at that time.' Across all NYC agencies, 'Did Not Observe'–style closures account for roughly 25% of 311 closures; the NYPD's share on residential noise specifically is higher. This dataset's resolution_description column is therefore where you read what the city actually did about each call — not just whether something was filed.

Of those, 2,132 (76%) close with 'DEP didn't observe a violation of the NYC Air or Noise Code,' 554 (20%) are flagged as duplicates of earlier complaints, and exactly 15 (0.53%) actually close with 'DEP observed a violation.' raw_evidence.label: The NYPD response pattern — 'observed no evidence of the violation'
raw_evidence.content: For residential, vehicle, and street noise the NYPD must physically observe an active violation to write a summons — and by the time officers arrive, the party is usually over. The first row in the raw CSV (case 56416252, January 1 2023, 12:00 AM, Sedgwick Avenue, Bronx) closed seventeen and a half hours later with the resolution text 'The Police Department responded to the complaint and with the information available observed no evidence of the violation at that time.' Across all NYC agencies, 'Did Not Observe'–style closures account for roughly 25% of 311 closures; the NYPD's share on residential noise specifically is higher. This dataset's resolution_description column is therefore where you read what the city actually did about each call — not just whether something was filed.

raw_evidence.label: Why this data became politically central — the NYPD Quality of Life Division
raw_evidence.content: On April 9, 2025 — shortly after the period this dataset covers — Mayor Eric Adams and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch launched a new NYPD Quality of Life Division ('Q-Teams') focused on noise, derelict vehicles, illegal mopeds, and other 311 complaint types. Officers received training on sound metering devices specifically for noise enforcement. The pilot improved non-emergency response times by 47 minutes on average citywide. By August 2025 Q-Teams were rolled out in every precinct in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island. The 2023–2024 noise data is the pre-Q-Team baseline; future cuts of the same dataset will show whether response times shortened and 'no evidence observed' closures fell after the division stood up.

raw_evidence.label: Borough-level YoY — Bronx complaints jumped 51%, Manhattan fell 3%
raw_evidence.content: The borough-level year-over-year change is enormous. The Bronx jumped from 141,303 to 213,606 complaints (+51.2%, +72,303 raw), more than the total volume swing for the rest of the city combined. Manhattan fell 3.1%, Queens fell 2.3%, Brooklyn grew 1.9%, and Staten Island grew 6.3%. The Bronx alone accounts for 108% of the citywide increase — every other borough except Brooklyn and Staten Island actually lost complaint volume. The vast majority of that Bronx jump is driven by ZIP 10466 (see ana_24).

raw_evidence.label: ZIP 10466 — one Bronx ZIP is 9% of all 2024 noise complaints
raw_evidence.content: ZIP 10466 (Wakefield / Williamsbridge in the north Bronx) accounts for 76,380 complaints over 2023+2024 — by far the most of any ZIP. The split between years is the headline: 8,809 in 2023, then 67,571 in 2024, a 7.67× increase in one calendar year. That 67,571 alone is 8.97% of every noise complaint filed in NYC in 2024 — from a ZIP code with roughly 62,049 residents (about 0.7% of the city's population). 93.4% (71,341) of 10466's complaints are 'Loud Music/Party.' Even compared to ana_11's per-capita ceiling, 10466 is in its own category.

raw_evidence.label: 311 launched in 2003 — the first call was a noise complaint
raw_evidence.content: New York City's 311 hotline was inaugurated by Mayor Michael Bloomberg on March 9, 2003 as the non-emergency counterpart to 911, consolidating roughly 40 city call centers and hotlines into a single number. The very first call to NYC311, at 12:01 AM on launch day, was a noise complaint from Jackson Heights, Queens. Through 2023 the system had received more than 525 million inquiries from New Yorkers, 68% by phone, 28% on the web, 3% in the mobile app (launched 2013), and the remainder through text and other channels. Every row in this dataset is one of those calls, web tickets, or app submissions — each one a New Yorker formally telling the city that something is too loud.
